subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 45-year-old man adopts a diet very high in protein. Within several days, hepatic urea production increases substantially. The rate-limiting reaction of the urea cycle is stimulated by N-acetylglutamate, whose concentration rises after a protein-rich meal.
question: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
explanation_correct: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I catalyzes the condensation of ammonia and bicarbonate to carbamoyl phosphate in the mitochondrial matrix, consuming two ATP, and it is the rate-limiting enzyme of ureagenesis. N-acetylglutamate is its obligate allosteric activator, and CPS I activity rises with dietary protein intake.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyzes the next step, carbamoyl phosphate plus ornithine to citrulline, but it is not the rate-limiting or N-acetylglutamate-regulated step.
explanation_incorrect.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase incorporates aspartate into the cycle but is not the rate-limiting enzyme of ureagenesis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Arginase catalyzes the final step, releasing urea and ornithine; it does not initiate the cycle.
explanation_incorrect.E: N-acetylglutamate synthase produces the allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I but does not catalyze a step of urea formation itself.

educationalObjective: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the rate-limiting, N-acetylglutamate-activated enzyme of the urea cycle.
